messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Nadia Rahman was 32 when she came for treatment, a divorced South Asian American woman who worked as a hospital chaplain and had built much of her identity around being able to sit with other people’s pain and help them name it. What happened to her was torture during a period of detention overseas while she was visiting extended family. In the first session she tried several times to describe it and each time seemed to arrive at the edge of the memory and stall. She would say she knew exactly what had happened, that it was all there, but when she tried to tell it in order, the words seemed to fall away. She lost the thread mid-sentence, pressed her fingers hard into the arms of the chair, and shook her head as if language itself had become unreliable. What remained most vividly were sensory fragments: men in uniform standing over her, the scrape of boots, the metallic clatter of doors, hands pinning her wrists and shoulders when she struggled, the unbearable certainty of being physically overpowered. The memory lived in her as something she could feel and hear more easily than speak.

In the months after she returned home, Nadia found that the parts she could not put into words were often the parts that surged up most forcefully in daily life. A clipped command in a security officer’s voice at the hospital entrance, the sight of police uniforms in the emergency department, or the sound of keys and heavy shoes in a corridor could bring her to a sudden stop. If someone brushed past her in a crowd or she felt hemmed in between people in an elevator, her body reacted before she could explain to herself why; she would go rigid, breathless, with the old sense of being held down returning in full force. What frightened her was that these reactions felt tied to something she knew had happened yet could not narrate clearly. Because the memory came back as sound, pressure, and image rather than a story she could tell herself, those same sounds, sensations, and uniforms in the present hit her with a terrifying immediacy.

Her work as a chaplain made these encounters hard to avoid. She moved through hospital corridors where security staff were posted, crossed open atriums and exposed parking areas between buildings, and was expected to approach families and staff she had once known as part of her ordinary pastoral rounds. Over time she began altering her routes through the hospital to avoid large open lobbies where she felt visible and undefended. She lingered in side hallways, took service elevators, and timed her movements to reduce the chance of passing uniformed personnel. Outside work she stopped meeting people she had socialized with before the detention, partly because their questions invited explanation and partly because she could not bear the shame of freezing when asked what had happened. On the worst evenings, when the unformed memory pressed in and she could not stop hearing the sounds or feeling the restraint in her body, she would hurt herself in small, controlled ways just to force her mind onto something immediate and physical.

These habits narrowed her life, but they also deepened the very problem she was trying to escape. The less Nadia entered open spaces, saw familiar people, or allowed herself to stay with the sensory fragments long enough to speak about them, the more unreachable the event became in words. She had come to believe that if she started describing it, she would lose control completely, and each retreat confirmed that belief. Even in therapy she circled around the torture rather than through it, offering isolated details and then falling silent, as though avoidance had taught the memory to remain nonverbal. After cutting herself, she would sometimes feel briefly steadier, but afterward she was even less able to explain what had overwhelmed her in the first place.

By the time she sought help, the strain was showing at work. She was still able to sit beside dying patients and pray with families, but internally she was scanning constantly for uniforms, footsteps, enclosed passages, and any moment of unwanted contact. Colleagues had noticed that she disappeared from common areas and turned down shared lunches. She was frightened by how quickly her world was shrinking and by the possibility that she might no longer be able to do the work that mattered most to her. What finally brought her in was not only the intensity of the reactions, but the fear that the torture had taken from her the very thing she relied on most: the capacity to make suffering speakable. She said she wanted help finding words, and she was terrified that if she could not, the sounds and sensations would go on ruling her life.
